summary: Defines an extension to the IPv6 multicast addressing architecture in which a multicast address is built from a network's unicast prefix. A network that receives a unicast prefix automatically gets its own multicast addresses, without needing an inter-domain allocation protocol. It was later updated by RFCs 3956, 4489 and 7371.

eli5.summary: If you own a street, you automatically own all the mailbox numbers on it. Likewise, a network that owns an address block gets its own group-broadcast addresses without asking anyone else.

subtitle: How an IPv6 multicast address can embed a network's unicast prefix so a network gets its own multicast addresses.

tldr.problem: IPv6 multicast addressing had no built-in support for dynamic address allocation, and the IPv4-style approach needs a multi-layered, multi-protocol system.
tldr.mechanism: A new multicast address format carries the owner's unicast network prefix and its length, with a P flag marking such addresses. Whoever is delegated a unicast prefix can then work out its own multicast addresses.
tldr.outcome: Operators need not run an inter-domain allocation protocol. Setting the prefix and its length to zero also gives the source-specific multicast range FF3x::/32. The RFC was updated by RFC 3956, RFC 4489 and RFC 7371.

today: RFC 3306 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 3956, RFC 4489 and RFC 7371, so read those updates alongside it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 3306 extends the multicast part of the IPv6 addressing architecture defined in RFC 2373. The existing architecture has no built-in support for dynamic address allocation. This specification puts information into the multicast address itself so that IPv6 multicast addresses, and IPv6 source-specific multicast addresses, can be allocated dynamically.
sections.eli5: Group addresses used to be handed out with no system. This RFC hides a clue about the owner inside the address, so handing them out becomes easy.

sections.title: Motivation
sections.content:
The IPv4 multicast address allocation architecture (RFC 2908) is a multi-layered, multi-protocol system. The goal here is to reduce the number of protocols that must be deployed to get dynamic multicast address allocation.

Unicast prefix-based allocation removes, at a minimum, the need to run the Multicast Address Allocation Protocol (AAP) and the Multicast Address-Set Claim (MASC) protocol (RFC 2909). By delegating multicast addresses at the same time as unicast prefixes, operators can identify their multicast addresses without an inter-domain allocation protocol.
sections.eli5: Instead of a big committee deciding who gets which group address, you get yours together with your network address.

sections.title: The Multicast Address Format
sections.content:
The existing format is 8 bits of 11111111, 4 flag bits, 4 scope bits and a 112-bit group ID. The new format keeps the first three fields and splits the rest: an 8-bit reserved field, an 8-bit plen, a 64-bit network prefix and a 32-bit group ID.

The four flags are 0 0 P T. P = 0 means the address is not assigned based on the network prefix (an ordinary address as in RFC 2373). P = 1 means it is. If P = 1, T MUST be set to 1.

  • reserved MUST be zero.
  • plen is the number of bits in the network prefix field that identify the subnet when P = 1.
  • network prefix holds the unicast prefix of the domain owning, or allocating, the address. Non-significant bits SHOULD be zero. The interface identifier rules limit the prefix to at most 64 bits.
  • group ID follows the guidelines of RFC 3307.

The scope of the address MUST NOT exceed the scope of the embedded unicast prefix.
sections.eli5: The address has labelled boxes. One box holds a copy of your network's address, one says how long that copy is, and the rest says which group inside your network.

sections.title: Address Lifetime
sections.content:
The lifetime of a unicast prefix-based multicast address SHOULD NOT exceed the Valid Lifetime in the Prefix Information option for the unicast prefix, carried in the Neighbor Discovery Router Advertisement (RFC 2461). The lifetime is needed to support the Abstract API for Multicast Address Allocation (RFC 2771).

The advertised Valid Lifetime does not mean the prefix will expire when it runs out. It is typically a constant until a renumbering event is scheduled, after which the prefix does become invalid. Using these multicast addresses after the prefix is invalid may cause operational problems, for example routers that compare the multicast prefix against the prefix assigned to an AS may discard the packet.
sections.eli5: Your group addresses are only good while your street address is good. If the street gets renamed, the old group addresses may stop working.

sections.title: Source-Specific Multicast Addresses
sections.content: The format supports source-specific multicast addresses. To create one, a node MUST set P = 1, plen = 0 and network prefix = 0. These settings yield the SSM range FF3x::/32, where x is any valid scope value. The source address field in the IPv6 header identifies the owner of the multicast address.
sections.eli5: If you set the street part to nothing, the address becomes a channel that only a named sender can use, and the sender's own address tells you who owns it.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content: A network with the unicast prefix 3FFE:FFFF:1::/48 has the unicast prefix-based multicast prefix FF3x:0030:3FFE:FFFF:0001::/96, where x is any valid scope. All IPv6 SSM multicast addresses have the format FF3x::/96.
sections.eli5: Copy the network's address into the middle of the group address, and the group address is ready to use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The embedded unicast prefix can help identify the allocation domain of a multicast address. However, a domain that wants to avoid being traced can create addresses with a prefix not assigned to it, or with a smaller scope embedded prefix.

Source-specific multicast addresses can sometimes help prevent denial-of-service attacks by arbitrary sources, though no guarantee is provided. The security considerations for SSM are discussed in more depth in the SSM architecture document.
sections.eli5: The hidden clue can show who owns a group address, but a sneaky owner can leave a false clue.
